newsitem.title: FRANCE: France urges nationals to quit Zaire, sends troops.
newsitem.headline: France urges nationals to quit Zaire, sends troops.

text.p: In a sign of growing concern about the crisis in Zaire, France urged its citizens on Thursday to leave the country and sent extra troops and planes to neighbouring states in case it has to protect them.

"Given the situation, and in order to ensure the safety of our citizens if necessary, the Ministry of Defence has decided to send extra resources to Libreville and Brazzaville," Defence Ministry spokesman Pierre Servent told a briefing.
France also renewed its call for a ceasefire and a negotiated settlement to the rebellion gaining ground rapidly from the east of the sprawling central African country.

It made no mention of veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, a longtime French protege, whose son said he planned to return to Zaire from France on Friday, following renewed cancer treatment in Monaco, to seek a political solution to the crisis.

"We remain convinced that the Zairean crisis can only be solved by associating all political forces in a consensual electoral process," French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters. But in an acknowledgement that such a settlement appears remote, he advised French nationals to leave Zaire.
"The French authorities recommend that citizens whose presence is not essential leave the country temporarily. This precaution applies particularly to families," he said.
Rebels led by opposition politician Laurent Kabila have captured more than one-fifth of Zaire, including its third-biggest city, Kisangani, routing a demoralised army.
The relentless rebel advance has sparked fears of violence or a coup in Kinshasa to overthrow the ailing Mobutu.
"Mobutu is nothing any more and everybody knows it," one French government Africa-watcher said in a particularly blunt private assessment. "The Zairean army no longer exists."

Defence ministry officials said three transport planes -- two C160 Transals and a C130 Hercules -- and two Puma helicopters were flown to the Gabonese capital Libreville during the night with 40 extra soldiers.
They join the 600 troops France keeps based in oil-producing Gabon.
Another 60 soldiers will go on to the Congolese capital Brazzaville, across the Zaire river from Kinshasa, they said.
Rummelhardt said there were about 1,500 French citizens in Zaire, more than 900 of them in Kinshasa.
The military deployment and the travel advisory were both described as precautions.
France put in place a similar deployment last November, but withdrew it discreetly in December when the initial panic caused by the rebels' first victories in eastern Zaire calmed down.
Paris sent troops to Kinshasa to protect and evacuate foreign nationals in 1991 and 1993 when unpaid army soldiers rampaged through the capital and other cities.
